newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi sees possible action in pay dispute.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi sees possible action in pay dispute.

text.p: Italian trade union federations on Friday threatened retaliation if the government failed to act in a metalworkers' pay dispute and Prime Minister Romano Prodi said Rome would intervene directly if such action was useful.

Engineering and metal workers staged strikes throughout Italy in the bitter wrangle with employers' association Federmeccanica on renewing contracts, after employers presented a list of demands deemed "unacceptable" by unions.
Workers downed tools for two hours in the northern cities of Milan and Turin, demonstrated in the port city of Genoa and blocked traffic in the southern city of Taranto.

Italy's three largest trades union federations CGIL, CISL and UIL swung their weight behind the FIOM, FIM and UILM metal workers' unions, threatening action if the government failed to intervene effectively.

"The union will react extremely harshly towards Federmeccanica and (employers' umbrella association) Confindustria in order to defend the contracts," a joint statement from the union federations and the engineering unions said.
"It will consider any government decision not to present a conclusive proposal, as is its duty, as an act of hostility and will act accordingly even through confrontation."
Prodi, speaking at an end-of-year news conference, said the dispute over salary levels in the labour contracts had reached a "very delicate" phase.
He said the government would intervene directly when such action "could be useful in unblocking a situation that has become bogged down".
Labour Minister Tiziano Treu, talking after a meeting with union leaders, said the government was studying what it could do and would say soon how it proposed to act.
Treu said the government was extremely concerned about the document presented by Federmeccanica.

The unions representing 1.7 million workers in the metalworking and engineering sectors, which account for 40 percent of total manufacturing output in Italy, are in dispute over how much money should be included in 1996-1998 contracts for loss of purchasing power in the past two years.
Treu has been holding separate talks this week with trades unions and Federmeccanica but is not so far mediating formally.

Negotiations faltered on Thursday after Federmeccanica presented Treu with a list of conditions for an accord, including a demand for commitment from the government to contain labour costs and for special measures for the poor south.
Unions condemned the proposals as unacceptable and called the two hour strikes for Friday.
The metalworkers' contracts expired in June and unions have held two other national strikes in support of their claim.
